features.title: nān and ne
features.description: Nān means no one when used alone, and no in nān mann. Keep ne with the finite verb: the two negatives express one negation. These exact forms support26.2,26.3 and27.4; the larger negative-pronoun family remains unassigned.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: būtan ðurh
features.description: Use the supplied connector būtan, except, before ðurh plus an accusative phrase. The through construction is prior; exact source spelling ðurh is supplied beside taught þurh. This is not the earlier būtan+dative without construction.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: cwæð tō him
features.description: Use supplied cwæð tō him, said to him: tō names the speech addressee and governs dative him. Cook159 opens Se Hǣlend cwæð tō ðǣm wǣdlan; Cook153 also has Cwæð hē, se biscop, him tō, whose postposition §201.1 explains. This local adaptation leaves the earlier exact postposed sense record unchanged. The direct quotation is already taught; no full new recipient system is inferred.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: rīnde hit
features.description: Rīnde is the supplied third-singular preterite rained, with impersonal hit, it. The weakI dental form is derived from rīnan; no complete independent rain paradigm is assigned.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: scīnende
features.description: Scīnende means shining, a supplied present participle agreeing with neuter singular rēaf. Keep it with the description of the raiment; its presence does not establish a compulsory English-style progressive system.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: hrēosende; tō nāhte
features.description: Hrēosende is falling, nominative masculine singular, describing munt. Weorðan tō nāhte means come to nothing; nāhte is the supplied form in this fixed result expression. No full nāht declension or negative family is assigned.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: swā-swā
features.description: Swā-swā is the supplied like/as connector. The following ān plus genitive ðissa uses the already taught one-of-a-group construction.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: on eallum his wuldre
features.description: The bounded expression on eallum his wuldre means in all his glory. On governs the dative group here; eallum agrees with neuter wuldre, while his names the possessor. The earlier supplied glory-expression history remains supplied.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: gelamp … ðæt
features.description: Gelamp is the supplied singular past happened. A following ðæt-clause states what happened; optional introductory hit is anticipatory. The content of the clause is past indicative here, not automatically subjunctive because it follows ðæt.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: feorran
features.description: Feorran is the supplied adverb from afar. Its ending already expresses the from sense; an extra of is not required.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: gemun … ðæt
features.description: Gemun is the supplied singular command remember. In this local command a following ðæt-clause recalls an asserted past fact, using the newly taught onfēnge received. No whole new preterite-present system is assigned.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: on ðīnum līfe
features.description: The exact on ðīnum līfe means in/during your life. The lifetime group is dative singular. This local expression is supported by Cook159 on woruldlīfe, in earthly life, with the ordinary dative lifetime noun and agreeing possessive substituted. It is not inferred solely from earlier physical location or a specific weekday use of on.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: ðēah hwā … ārīse
features.description: Hwā has the supplied indefinite sense anyone in this concessive clause. The explicitly taught ārīse is present subjunctive; preserve the requested final-verb placement. Familiar interrogative hwā did not establish this indefinite use.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: habbað … licgende
features.description: Licgende means lying, accusative masculine plural describing the object Lazaras. In this supported construction habbað has the people as its accusative object and the participle describes their situation at the gates. This does not assign a new general habban-plus-participle system.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: on Godes ðearfum
features.description: In the exact acquire-friends expression on Godes ðearfum means in/among God’s poor. The group after on is dative plural; Godes is its internal dependent genitive. This local domain use is supplied and does not add a general new sense to every on phrase.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: æt his geate; æt ēowrum geatum
features.description: Use æt with dative place: æt his geate at his gate, æt ēowrum geatum at your gates. His is the personal genitive possessor; ēowrum agrees with plural geatum. The exact at sense remains locally supplied, even though the form æt is already productive in another frame.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: Opening passive and proportion
features.description: Ymbseald means surrounded/beset; mid introduces the surrounding dangers. Efne reinforces the assertion. The paired swā clauses with comparatives mean the greater the worldly dignities, the fiercer the dangers. This proportional construction remains supported, distinct from prior equal-degree swā…swā.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: Examples recognized and understood
features.description: Be ðǣm is a separate dative prepositional phrase, by/from that: it points back to the preceding proposition as the basis for inference. Bȳsena is the accusative examples governed by the two modal infinitives oncnāwan and ongietan. The paired verbs reinforce one act of understanding; do not treat bȳsena as dative because be appears earlier.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: Tree, growth, result and reflexive
features.description: The relative ðe identifies the tree. Wiexð is the exact source third singular grows, beside the earlier selected wiext. The result clause ðæt hit hlīfað explains how it grows: so that it towers above the other trees. Brǣt hit means spreads itself; this hit is accusative and refers to the same tree. The first hit in the result clause is its nominative subject.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: Storm and passive comparison
features.description: Sęmninga is suddenly. Gestęnt is singular present, assails/comes on; Cook’s note identifies storm and the following strong wind as its two subjects. Preserve the singular Old English wording; idiomatic English can use plural strike. The two following ðonne tokens function differently: then in the temporal correlation and than after swīðlicor more violently. Gewǣged and geswęnged are supplied passive bases. Se ōðer wudu means the rest of the forest, as the original note says.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: Original157n3: hruron
features.description: Cook asks for the indicative preterite plural of hrēosan. Supply hruron (all plural persons); the classII plural uses u with s/r alternation. This is reference-only help, not a new complete productive hrēosan paradigm or an unaided recall task.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: Cliffs and coordinated infinitives
features.description: Swā bið ēac gelīce be… means it is likewise also with/concerning…. The plural hīe refers to the cliffs/crags. Hlīfiað means tower and feorr ūp far up. Onginnað begin governs both feallan and hrēosan; full strengthens ðearlice, very violently. The two fall verbs can reinforce one collapse rather than name two chronologically separate events. Tō eorðan gives the destination to the earth.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: ðā-ðe
features.description: Ðā-ðe is the exact joined source spelling of plural relative ðā with ðe, which. It is nominative plural as subject of standað and refers to muntum and dūnum. The prior compound-relative construction is reused with this explicitly supplied spelling; no new headword or unrestricted joining rule is inferred.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: Mountains and punishment
features.description: Supply the repeated it is likewise with/concerning after Swilce ēac. Hēah is adverbial high with standað. Ðā-hwæðre means nevertheless. The mountains pay the penalty of their pre-eminence: the ðæt-clause explains that penalty. Geneahhe is often, preserving the source’s unmarked spelling beside dictionary genēahhe. Geðrēade, geðrǣste and geslægene are agreeing plural passive participles: punished/battered/struck by heavenly fire and thunderbolts. These exact forms do not assign three full new paradigms.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

features.title: The human conclusion
features.description: The first subject is the high powers; hrēosað and feallað reinforce their fall, and weorðað tō lore means come to destruction. The second subject is the wealth of this world, which becomes sorrow (tō sorge). The third is these earthly wonders, which come to nothing (tō nāhte). The tō-result expressions are supplied; they are not instances of the earlier nominative-predicate become frame.
features.scope_note: Whole local expression supported with help visible throughout the task; no unrestricted new syntax or unaided recall.

This does not assign a new general habban-plus-participle system.

cook_support.title: on Godes ðearfum
cook_support.text: In the exact acquire-friends expression on Godes ðearfum means in/among God’s poor. The group after on is dative plural; Godes is its internal dependent genitive. This local domain use is supplied and does not add a general new sense to every on phrase.

cook_support.title: æt his geate; æt ēowrum geatum
cook_support.text: Use æt with dative place: æt his geate at his gate, æt ēowrum geatum at your gates. His is the personal genitive possessor; ēowrum agrees with plural geatum. The exact at sense remains locally supplied, even though the form æt is already productive in another frame.

reading_support.title: Opening passive and proportion
reading_support.text: Ymbseald means surrounded/beset; mid introduces the surrounding dangers. Efne reinforces the assertion. The paired swā clauses with comparatives mean the greater the worldly dignities, the fiercer the dangers. This proportional construction remains supported, distinct from prior equal-degree swā…swā.

reading_support.title: Examples recognized and understood
reading_support.text: Be ðǣm is a separate dative prepositional phrase, by/from that: it points back to the preceding proposition as the basis for inference. Bȳsena is the accusative examples governed by the two modal infinitives oncnāwan and ongietan. The paired verbs reinforce one act of understanding; do not treat bȳsena as dative because be appears earlier.

reading_support.title: Tree, growth, result and reflexive
reading_support.text: The relative ðe identifies the tree. Wiexð is the exact source third singular grows, beside the earlier selected wiext. The result clause ðæt hit hlīfað explains how it grows: so that it towers above the other trees. Brǣt hit means spreads itself; this hit is accusative and refers to the same tree. The first hit in the result clause is its nominative subject.

reading_support.title: Storm and passive comparison
reading_support.text: Sęmninga is suddenly. Gestęnt is singular present, assails/comes on; Cook’s note identifies storm and the following strong wind as its two subjects. Preserve the singular Old English wording; idiomatic English can use plural strike. The two following ðonne tokens function differently: then in the temporal correlation and than after swīðlicor more violently. Gewǣged and geswęnged are supplied passive bases. Se ōðer wudu means the rest of the forest, as the original note says.

reading_support.title: Original157n3: hruron
reading_support.text: Cook asks for the indicative preterite plural of hrēosan. Supply hruron (all plural persons); the classII plural uses u with s/r alternation. This is reference-only help, not a new complete productive hrēosan paradigm or an unaided recall task.

reading_support.title: Cliffs and coordinated infinitives
reading_support.text: Swā bið ēac gelīce be… means it is likewise also with/concerning…. The plural hīe refers to the cliffs/crags. Hlīfiað means tower and feorr ūp far up. Onginnað begin governs both feallan and hrēosan; full strengthens ðearlice, very violently. The two fall verbs can reinforce one collapse rather than name two chronologically separate events. Tō eorðan gives the destination to the earth.

reading_support.title: ðā-ðe
reading_support.text: Ðā-ðe is the exact joined source spelling of plural relative ðā with ðe, which. It is nominative plural as subject of standað and refers to muntum and dūnum. The prior compound-relative construction is reused with this explicitly supplied spelling; no new headword or unrestricted joining rule is inferred.

reading_support.title: Mountains and punishment
reading_support.text: Supply the repeated it is likewise with/concerning after Swilce ēac. Hēah is adverbial high with standað. Ðā-hwæðre means nevertheless. The mountains pay the penalty of their pre-eminence: the ðæt-clause explains that penalty. Geneahhe is often, preserving the source’s unmarked spelling beside dictionary genēahhe. Geðrēade, geðrǣste and geslægene are agreeing plural passive participles: punished/battered/struck by heavenly fire and thunderbolts. These exact forms do not assign three full new paradigms.

reading_support.title: The human conclusion
reading_support.text: The first subject is the high powers; hrēosað and feallað reinforce their fall, and weorðað tō lore means come to destruction. The second subject is the wealth of this world, which becomes sorrow (tō sorge). The third is these earthly wonders, which come to nothing (tō nāhte). The tō-result expressions are supplied; they are not instances of the earlier nominative-predicate become frame.
